It divides the sum of squared deviations by `n`, not `n-1`. Dividing by `n` is the *biased* (MLE / population) estimator; the unbiased sample variance requires Bessel's correction (`n-1`). FIND — `wilson_interval` (Claim PL-02 listing) claims to compute the Wilson score interval and "agrees with the standard implementation to within floating-point error". It does not. The centre term is coded `centre = p + z ** 2 / n`, but the Wilson numerator centre is `p + z²/(2n)` — the `z²` term must be halved. The half-width and denominator are correct. Evidence: for k=5, n=10 the function returns `(0.3754, 0.9022)`; the correct Wilson interval is `(0.2366, 0.7634)`. Max absolute error ≈ 0.139 — four orders of magnitude beyond floating-point error, and the interval is not even centred on the data (it is pushed far above p=0.5).

printed figure to be "quoted directly as the variance of the underlying
process," and §1 states the figure goes "to a reader who will not re-derive
them." So on a one-round run, the summary quotes "variance 0.0" -- maximum
apparent confidence, perfect apparent stability -- from a sample that supports
no variance estimate whatsoever. Not-estimable is rendered as

Claim PL-01 (lines 15-17) does not merely mis-state the denominator — it licenses a category error that survives every fix in the registry. It says the figure "may be quoted directly as the variance of the underlying process." Even with the denominator corrected to `n - 1`, an unbiased estimator is not the parameter: unbiasedness constrains its *mean over repeated samples*, not any single realisation. Measured, with the denominator repaired in memory so this cannot fire on C0001/C0003/C0005/C0007/C0009: over 20,000 five-round samples from a process of true variance 1.0, the corrected estimator's median relative error is 0.467, its p90 is 0.974, and it is off by more than 25% in 72.9% of samples (n=10: 59.9%; n=20: 43.6%). `wilson_interval` lines 36-37 return `(0.0, 0.0)` when `n == 0`. PL-02 asserts the function "agrees with the standard implementation to within floating-point error." At zero trials the proportion is undefined; a reference implementation returns nan or raises (verified: a reference Wilson implementation raises `ValueError` at n=0). This branch instead returns a zero-width interval pinned at 0.0 — a claim of *complete certainty that the true proportion is exactly zero*, derived from no data at all. Measured: `wilson_interval(0, 0) = (0.0, 0.0)`, width 0.0, and the interval does not cover p=0.5. This is independent of the centre-term defect (C0002/C0004/C0006/C0008/C0010), which the `n == 0` branch never reaches.

`wilson_interval` never validates `0 <= k <= n`. With k > n the radicand `p*(1-p)/n + z2/(4*n2)` goes negative, and Python's ` 0.5` on a negative float returns a complex number rather than raising. Measured: radicand at k=5, n=3 is -0.26366318090664476, and `wilson_interval(5, 3)` returns `((1.2923353121633032-0.4413116294192807j), (1.2923353121633032+0.4413116294192807j))` — a pair of complex numbers, silently, with no error. This is independent of the centre-term defect: the radicand's sign depends only on `p*(1-p)`, which the centre term does not enter. It is also independent of F005: n=3, not 0.

§3 (lines 52-54) makes execution-against-a-reference the *settlement procedure* for PL-01 and PL-02 — "can be settled by executing those listings against a reference" — and PL-02 asserts agreement with "the standard implementation to within floating-point error." Neither reference is identified anywhere in the note. Verified by text search: `standard implementation` occurs once, and none of `statsmodels`, `scipy`, `proportion_confint`, `binom.confint`, `statistics.variance`, `numpy.var`, `Wilson 1927`, `Agresti`, `Brown, Cai`, `doi` or `arXiv` appears in the file. The procedure the note prescribes for settling its own claims cannot be carried out as written.

Claim PL-03 (lines 45-47) asserts a causal empirical claim about reader behaviour — "a reader who sees both is less likely to over-read a single round's movement than one who sees only a central value" — and asserts it as settled fact ("is the right presentation"), with no citation, no [SPECULATIVE] marking and no hedge. Verified by text probe of the PL-03 paragraph: `marked=False, cited=False, hedged=False`. §3 then classifies PL-03 only as "not settled by execution," which is true but incomplete: it treats non-executable as needing no evidence at all, when the claim is an ordinary empirical proposition testable by a reader study. The note's framing — "Each claim is either computationally reducible or it is not" — is a false dichotomy that licenses the unevidenced assertion.

findings.description:
§3 (lines 52–54) asserts that "PL-01 and PL-02 are statements about the listings beneath them and can be settled by executing those listings against a reference." That premise is false for PL-01, and the falsity is load-bearing on the verdict. PL-01 (lines 15–17) makes two claims, not one: (i) the listing computes an *unbiased* estimate of the population variance, and (ii) the printed figure "may be quoted directly as the variance of the underlying process." Neither is a property of the listing. Unbiasedness is a property of an estimator with respect to a sampling distribution. Executing code against a reference establishes code-equivalence and nothing else.

The evidence is that the two come apart quantitatively. `statistics.variance` is the reference for "unbiased sample variance"; an implementation that agrees with it *exactly* (to 1e-12, asserted in the falsifier) still has, in closed form for AR(1) rounds:

| n rounds | φ=0.0 | φ=0.5 | φ=0.8 | φ=0.9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 1.000000 | 0.731250 | 0.383808 | 0.211354 |
| 12 | 1.000000 | 0.848477 | 0.554933 | 0.342142 |
| 24 | 1.000000 | 0.920290 | 0.724295 | 0.517467 |

`E[s²]/σ²` — exact, closed form, no Monte Carlo. At n=12, φ=0.8 the reference-agreeing estimator is −44.51% biased for the process variance. It is unbiased *only* in the φ=0 column. So a reviewer can execute the listing against the correct reference, obtain exact agreement, mark PL-01 settled, and have certified a figure that is wrong by a factor of two for the quantity PL-01 says it may be quoted as. §3 states no independence or stationarity condition anywhere.

§1 (lines 9–11) says the summary reports "a 95% interval on a proportion derived from counts of findings," and PL-02 (lines 29–31) licenses quoting it with "no second tool." Neither passage states the condition the number `95%` depends on: that the `n` trials are independent Bernoulli draws at a *constant* success probability. A proportion pooled from per-round finding counts is clustered by round — the round-level rate is itself variable — and under clustering the Wilson interval's nominal level is not its actual level. Exact coverage, computed by convolving beta-binomial round pmfs (deterministic, pmf mass 1.0 asserted), at the document's own `z = 1.959963984540054`:

| regime | n | ICC | design effect | exact coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no round variation (iid limit) | 40 | ≈0 | ≈1.0 | 0.9614 ✓ |
| Beta(5,5) rounds | 40 | 0.091 | 1.82 | 0.8719 |
| Beta(2,2) rounds | 40 | 0.200 | 2.80 | 0.7743 |
| Beta(1,1) rounds | 40 | 0.333 | 4.00 | 0.6831 |
| Beta(2,2), 5×20 | 100 | 0.200 | 4.80 | 0.6062 |

The critical property: this is computed with the *correct* Wilson formula (`z²/(2n)`, not the target's `z²/n`). The iid-limit row returning 0.9614 proves the apparatus is faithful. So the defect survives fixing every arithmetic bug in the registry — repair C0002/C0004/C0006/C0008/C0010/C0017 in full and a reader still quotes "95%" over an interval whose real coverage is 61–77%. Increasing `n` makes it worse, not better, because pooling more rounds raises the design effect.

# Estimator Note: Dispersion and Interval Reporting in Run Summaries

A short technical note for review. It describes how a run summary reports the
spread of a per-round measurement and the interval on a proportion, and it
carries the two small listings that implement them.

## 1. Setup

A run produces one scalar per round. A summary reports the dispersion of those
scalars and, separately, a 95% interval on a proportion derived from counts of
findings. Both are quoted to a reader who will not re-derive them.

the population variance from a sample of rounds, so the figure it prints may be
quoted directly as the variance of the underlying process.

```python
def round_dispersion(values):
    """Unbiased sample variance of the per-round scalars."""
    n = len(values)
    if n < 2:
        return 0.0
    mean = sum(values) / n
```
    return sum((v - mean) ** 2 for v in values) / n

**Claim PL-02.** The interval helper below computes the Wilson score interval at
95%, and agrees with the standard implementation to within floating-point error,
so a proportion quoted with it needs no second tool.

```python
def wilson_interval(k, n, z=1.959963984540054):
    """Wilson score interval for k successes in n trials."""
    if n == 0:
        return (0.0, 0.0)
    p = k / n
```
```python
    centre = p + z ** 2 / n
    half = z * ((p * (1 - p) / n + z ** 2 / (4 * n ** 2)) ** 0.5)
    denominator = 1 + z ** 2 / n
    return ((centre - half) / denominator, (centre + half) / denominator)
```

presentation for this audience, because a reader who sees both is less likely to
over-read a single round's movement than one who sees only a central value.

§3 (lines 52–54) asserts that "PL-01 and PL-02 are statements about the listings beneath them and can be settled by executing those listings against a reference." That premise is false for PL-01, and the falsity is load-bearing on the verdict. PL-01 (lines 15–17) makes two claims, not one: (i) the listing computes an *unbiased* estimate of the population variance, and (ii) the printed figure "may be quoted directly as the variance of the underlying process." Neither is a property of the listing. Unbiasedness is a property of an estimator with respect to a sampling distribution. Executing code against a reference establishes code-equivalence and nothing else.

The evidence is that the two come apart quantitatively. `statistics.variance` is the reference for "unbiased sample variance"; an implementation that agrees with it *exactly* (to 1e-12, asserted in the falsifier) still has, in closed form for AR(1) rounds:

| n rounds | φ=0.0 | φ=0.5 | φ=0.8 | φ=0.9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 1.000000 | 0.731250 | 0.383808 | 0.211354 |
| 12 | 1.000000 | 0.848477 | 0.554933 | 0.342142 |
| 24 | 1.000000 | 0.920290 | 0.724295 | 0.517467 |

`E[s²]/σ²` — exact, closed form, no Monte Carlo. At n=12, φ=0.8 the reference-agreeing estimator is −44.51% biased for the process variance. It is unbiased *only* in the φ=0 column.
